lessons.title: நாள் (nāḷ) — "day," the one this arc's Dravidian languages didn't lose
lessons.gloss: "day" — Tamil's everyday, native Dravidian word, already met inside "tomorrow"; unlike Kannada's dina, Telugu's rōju, and Malayalam's divasam, Tamil's plain day-word is NOT a loanword at all — நாள் just is the everyday word, no Sanskrit or Persian substitute doing that job

segments.text: You've now seen three Dravidian languages reach for a loanword — Sanskrit, twice, and Persian once — to name their everyday word for "day." Tamil doesn't. This lesson is about the one that didn't.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart - நாள் — genuinely native, genuinely everyday

segments.text: நாள் (nāḷ) — "day" — is native Dravidian, from Proto-Dravidian nāḷ. You've already met it, hiding inside நாளை (nāḷai, "tomorrow," Chapter 4). But here's the honest headline of this lesson: நாள் isn't a survivor clinging to one narrow sense the way some native Dravidian words are — it is simply Tamil's plain, everyday, unmarked word for counting a day, as ordinary as மூன்று நாள் (mūnṟu nāḷ, "three days").

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "nāḷ" — "day," native Dravidian, already met inside "tomorrow"]

segments.text: Where did you already meet நாள் before this lesson? (Inside நாளை, nāḷai, "tomorrow," Chapter 4.) Is Tamil's everyday day-word a loanword? (No — நாள் is native Dravidian.) Is it marginal or literary? (No — it is the plain everyday counting word.) Next: compare the other sisters' borrowed day-words and Tamil's formal tiṉam.

lessons.title: நாள் and தினம் — everyday native, formal borrowed
lessons.gloss: Tamil alone keeps a native everyday day-word while Sanskrit tiṉam occupies formal compounds

segments.text: Nāḷ is plainly native and everyday. Put that lexical choice beside the other Dravidian tracks.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: Four everyday day-words

segments.text: Tamil is the only one here whose unmarked everyday counting word remains native.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: Tamil still has தினம்

segments.text: தினம் (tiṉam) is the same Sanskrit dina as Kannada/Malayalam, ultimately from PIE dyew-, "shine," also behind Latin diēs. Tamil assigns it formal and compound work: சுதந்திர தினம், "Independence Day," and தினசரி, "daily." Casual counting remains nāḷ.
The language did not reject the loan; it gave native and borrowed forms different jobs.
Which track alone keeps a native everyday day-word? (Tamil.) Where does tiṉam appear? (Formal compounds.) Is it unrelated to Kannada dina? (No — it is the same Sanskrit tatsama.)
